text: You can now build, select, and combine arrays. This lesson puts them to work: summarizing data with totals, averages, and spreads. NumPy gives you these as built-in operations that run on a whole array at once, and they're the same statistics you'll meet again in the pandas and statistics chapters. The key new idea is the axis, which tells NumPy which direction to summarize.

Take a small table of weekly sales for three stores across four weeks. Call dot-sum on the whole array and you get 1595 total. Dot-mean gives you 132.92, the average cell. Dot-min and dot-max give you 80 and 200, the smallest and largest single sale. Each of these can be called as a method, like sales dot sum, or as a function, like np dot sum of sales — they're equivalent.

Without an axis, NumPy collapses the whole array into one number. With an axis, it collapses just one dimension — and the easiest way to remember it is that the axis you name is the one that disappears. Sum with axis equals 0 runs down the rows, giving you one total per week. Sum with axis equals 1 runs across the columns, giving you one total per store. If you know SQL, axis 0 is like a group-by-column total, and axis 1 is a row-wise total.

To find where the biggest value sits, use argmax. Without an axis, it returns a position in the flattened array — here, position 8. With an axis, it returns one position per row: 2, 1, 0. And np dot unravel underscore index converts that flat position back into row and column — position 8 turns out to be row 2, column 0: store three in week one, with 200, the biggest single sale in the table.

Averages describe the center of the data; standard deviation describes how spread out it is. Take order values where one big order sneaks in: 12, 15, 11, 18, 14, and 90. The mean comes out to 26.67, pulled way up by that outlier. The median, the middle value, comes out to 14.5 and barely notices it. When data has outliers, always compare both.

np dot std and np dot var divide by n by default, describing the data you actually have. When your data is a sample from a larger population, statisticians divide by n minus 1 instead — pass ddof equals 1 to do that, which bumps the standard deviation here from 28.41 up to 31.12. Watch out: pandas' dot-std method uses ddof equals 1 by default, while NumPy uses ddof equals 0 — that mismatch trips up a lot of beginners when results don't match between the two libraries.

A percentile tells you the value below which a given share of the data falls. np dot percentile of x at 25, 50, and 75 gives you the quartiles — 12.5, 14.5, and 17.25. np dot quantile of x at 0.9 gives you the 90th percentile, 54.0. Percentile takes numbers from 0 to 100; quantile takes fractions from 0 to 1 — and the 50th percentile is exactly the median.

To measure how two variables move together, use np dot corrcoef. It returns a matrix, and the off-diagonal entry is the correlation between the two inputs, ranging from negative 1 to 1. Comparing a small height and weight example gives a correlation of about 0.977 — close to 1, meaning the two rise together strongly. But correlation never proves that one causes the other, a point later statistics lessons come back to.

As the last lesson showed, nan poisons ordinary summaries — the mean of an array containing nan is nan itself, while np dot nanmean skips it and returns the real average, 2.0 here. A common preparation step for machine learning is standardizing: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, using the broadcasting you just learned. The result is a z-score, the number of standard deviations a value sits from the mean — our outlier, 90, stands out at 2.23 standard deviations above average.

To recap: sum, mean, min, max, and argmax summarize arrays, and the axis you name is the one that disappears. Compare mean and median to spot outliers, and use ddof equals 1 for a sample standard deviation. Percentile, quantile, and corrcoef describe position and relationships between variables. Use nanmean and friends for missing values, and z-scores to standardize. Next lesson: random numbers and simulation.
